So with this being an offering of a defense hedge outside of tech, how does this business model, specifically acquiring underperforming skilled nursing facilities, and then turning around the operations that drive it, how is that helping with its growth narrative?

So it's uh, definitely there in the data. Um, as you can see, uh, on the top here of this chart, it says, "I Own Nine Of The Top Ten Stocks for the second half of 2026. Uh, I think being that this is in the healthcare industry, when you enter market rotations and investors start rotating into safe-haven sectors and what they perceive as historically safe sectors, healthcare is one of the sectors that comes to the top of the list. And, certainly, the market has a lot of head- headwinds right now. So the healthcare sector has done well. Year-to-date, this stock is up about 16%, uh, and as you can see from the chart below, uh, towards the beginning of the year, we did have a, uh, Strong Buy on it, and when to Hold, and then the Strong Buy was resumed. Uh, so when you see that red, it means relative to the sector that it is a little bit rich, but one of my favorite metrics is called PEG, and that's where you combine value and growth together. And on that particular valuation metric, it's actually at about a 34- 34% discount to the sector. So I do like it.

NB: All right. Speaking of the Factor Grades, Steve, with PACS Group, how do these metrics reinforce the thesis that fundamental data ultimately outlasts short-term market volatility?

SC: Absolutely. Uh, companies that have good management teams or good businesses where the data comes in quarter after quarter, and it shows top-line growth, bottom-line growth, it shows that they're profitable. Investors always return to fundamentals. Sentiment, especially negative sentiment and anxiety, it tends to be short term in nature. It does have a big impact on the market because people will sell many stocks where they've made profits to put themselves into those safe-haven sectors as they panic based on fear and uncertainty.

But eventually, when you go through quarter after quarter of solid earnings, investors start to come around, then they return to those stocks with good fundamentals. So I imagine this will certainly be one of those cases. Uh, company beat expectations recently. Uh, they've been having a good growth stint for a while. So, uh, I don't think there's any reason to believe that that will change. And, uh, obviously, I mentioned the forward EBITA growth numbers- uh, of the EBIT numbers, and that is consensus forecast from Wall Street analysts. So that's not even our own model. We're taking consensus from analysts that are on Wall Street, and it looks like they're in good shape going forward.

NB: Well, I want to jump right over to our products that we have on site, our Alpha Picks portfolio, our Pro Quant portfolio, and our Quant Growth and Income portfolio. You know, and- and this chart right here, it breaks down really those key differences between all of the products. Now, keeping that in mind, how should an investor evaluate the differences in portfolio size, trade frequency, and even the stock universe when deciding which quantitative model fits their personal strategy?

SC: Yeah, I- I would say the common thread with all three of these is that it relies on the Seeking Alpha Quant System, which has a very good track record. So what it really comes down to with which one suits the individual really has to do with the frequency of ideas, um, how much bandwidth you have. So the Pro Quant portfolio is a fixed portfolio of 30 stocks, and it rebalances on a weekly basis. So every week, you could expect two to three new ideas. Alpha Picks, um, only two new ideas a month on the trading date closest to the 1st and the 15th. So these two portfolios, it really comes down to how often you want those ideas.

And then for the Quant and Growth Income, that has a portfolio of 30 stocks. It does have the same common thread that they have to be, uh, Quant Strong Buys or Buys, as with the other products, but the big difference with the Quant Growth and Income is each of those stocks pays a dividend. So it sort of has a dual mandate, which is capital appreciation and income generation. So the other two are based on the frequency of ideas that you want from our conventional quant model, and the Quant Growth and Income adds that income generation factor to it.

NB: All right. Now, I want to look at these numbers here. You know, all of our Quant portfolios continue to outperform their benchmarks. Now, given the seasonal volatility we've seen recently and all these broader market drawdowns, why does the historical data of these portfolios, specifically, favor staying the course over, you know, just selling during seasonal dips?

SC: Yeah, I think, you know, what we try to do with our quant system is ignore emotion, and we actually encourage investors and our subscribers to sort of take the emotional element out of investing. If I had a superpower, it would be to ignore the talking heads on TV and the many of the big headlines that you see, especially the ones that inflate risk and fear and uncertainty, and just stay disciplined. And that's what our quant system does, is, you know, on a daily basis, we're using data and we're looking for stocks that are collectively strong on growth, value, profitability, EPS revisions, and momentum.

And when we identify stocks that are collective on those traits, uh, those are the ones that we highlight as our Strong Buys. So, in essence, we're putting out stocks consistently that have good fundamentals. We look at the data. We don't pay attention to emotion. We don't pay attention to sentiment. However, I will say it does- it does often present good opportunities, cuz when stocks do weak on that fear and anxiety, it's usually a very opportune time to buy stocks with good fundamentals.

data.title: AVLV: Exploring Value In The U.S. Large Cap Universe
data.description:
American Century Investments-backed Avantis Investors has a wide range of low-cost thematic ETFs that could potentially fit anyone's portfolio, and the one we're going to learn about today is the Avantis U.S. Large Cap Value ETF (AVLV). I won't be analyzing it from an investing point of view, though. This article is a primer on this $22 billion fund that's been around, coming up on five years from September 21, 2021, and it's meant to familiarize you with how the ETF is constructed, what it's delivered so far, and what its long-term prospects look like.

What Is AVLV?

The ETF is focused on a single outcome, and that's long-term capital appreciation. You've probably figured out from the name that it tracks some value benchmark, and you're right. It's the Russell 1000 Value Index. You'll notice that the fund tracks the index pretty closely with its sub-2% tracking error and 7% annual turnover, but it only holds about 300 stocks.

The reason that's much fewer than what the index holds is the ETF's selection method. The index's constituents are put through a couple of filtration steps that involve profitability ratios and valuations. The ETF specifically looks at book to market value and profits to book value. Book value is just shareholder equity, so the ETF's sights are set on companies in the U.S. large-cap camp that are trading at discounts to equity and pre-tax earnings per dollar of book value.

That's the gist of what the ETF looks for, and that's built on top of what the index looks for, with some differences:

The index includes companies with relatively lower price to-book ratios, lower 2-year I/B/E/S forecast growth and lower historical 5-year sales growth. The index is reconstituted fully in June to ensure accurate representation of the US large cap value style, with updates for parent index membership changes in December and quarterly IPO inclusions in March and September. Since March 24, 2025, the index applies quarterly capping if constituent weights exceed target RIC thresholds. IPOs with investable market cap above the Russell Top 500 breakpoint are eligible for fast entry; breakpoints are set semi-annually and market-adjusted quarterly.

The ETF takes the whole index and applies its own valuation formulas to get to the final list of ~300 stocks. You're getting all of this in one basket at an expense ratio of 0.15%. There's a nominal yield of 1% that should more than cover the fees, if that's how you're thinking about it.

The holdings are pretty diverse, but what you want to do is make note of the top sectors. Financials, consumer discretionary, and energy make up more than half the ETF's assets, and that's something you always want to be aware of because a shift in the mix could mean completely different results.

Performance Since 2021

The ETF has done better than the benchmark, so the strategy it's been using definitely works. Or has worked. The last three years have been pretty good for the ETF.

We've got benchmark-beating performance, and that little bit of alpha being wrung out of the portfolio is a good sign that fund managers are working with a strategy that's proven itself over the AI supercycle we're in. We'll see what that looks like with the dividends reinvested, but let's also look at how AVLV's done against a pure Russell 1000 Value Index holding, which is what the iShares Russell 1000 Value ETF (IWD) is. I've also roped in Vanguard's Russell 1000 Value ETF (VONV).

I'll leave you to mull over that, because what I'd really like to get into is how this ETF is positioned going forward.

If you're looking at the decade ahead, I think value stocks rotating into prominence over the past year is a sign from the market that it can't absorb that much risk. You can see growth stocks (IWF) running flat, but value stocks (IWD) don't look like they saw the stop sign.

These are just signs. You're free to read them as you like. I'm just saying that an ETF with a value strategy could do well in the next decade. It's up to you to decide if it can or can't.

Summary

The ETF follows a strategy that's allowed it to beat the benchmark and other indexes over a 5-year period, and the risk seems to be lower than owning a broad, unfiltered set of large caps. The balance between pros and cons seems even. It's got a good grip on risk and value, and it's shown its shareholders that the methodology works. It's also a cheap way to have your portfolio risk managed by professionals.

I'm hoping this gives you a good springboard for your decision on AVLV. Be sure to look at the macro picture with as much objectivity as you can because good news on employment or a slowdown in inflation won't be that great for a value ETF. The market narrative can and will change based on economic developments, and having a balanced portfolio can be crucial when the narrative changes. For AVLV, the best counterfoil would be a growth fund.

Avantis has a couple of mutual funds (TNRAX) (TNXIX) that focus on the same market cap segment, and we're seeing these underperform the market as AVLV zooms ahead.

It's always a good idea to look for balanced opportunities when you're facing a macro environment that could go either way. With AVLV focused on value, there could be opportunities to balance your portfolio with a growth-focused fund and adjust the weightings based on the environment changes.

This article answers three questions about AVLV:

  • What is the best way for AVLV to work in a portfolio?
  • How is AVLV's portfolio constructed, and how are its sector allocation weightings?
  • How has AVLV performed against its benchmark in different investing environments?

Editor's note: This article is intended to provide a general overview of the ETF for educational purposes only and, unlike other articles on Seeking Alpha, does not offer an investment opinion about the ETF.
